title: Adani Wilmar Limited (AWL)
abstract: The total size of the edible oils market in India was estimated to be 13 million tons (mt) out of which imports amounted to about 4 mt. This made India the largest importer of edible oils in the world. Various edible oils are consumed in the India depending on the regional tastes and preferences. A differential in the duties on oil seed and oils made it favorable to import edible oils instead of oilseeds. Similarly, a differential duty between the refined oil and the raw oil encouraged the import of raw oil in order to support the domestic refineries. Adani Wilmar Limited (AWL) was a part of the Adani group, which started as a trading company mainly into exports of commodities. The group had recently entered into the infrastructure sector with the building of the Mundra port. The group had formed a joint venture with Wilmar Trading of Singapore to enter into the edible oil business. The company was setting up a re.nery with capacity of 600 tons per day. It planned to sell half of the production as bulk oil and the rest as packed oil. The company viewed supply chain management as one of the important means to get a competitive edge. Approximately 70% of the total logistics cost was accounted for by transportation cost. Some of the key decisions the company faced was the location of the warehouses, mode choice and routing.

summary.oneLiner: Case on Adani Wilmar's edible oil venture in India, where duties and transport costs shape warehouse, mode and routing decisions.
summary.overview: This case covers Adani Wilmar Limited, a joint venture between the Adani group and Wilmar Trading of Singapore, entering India's edible oil business. India was the world's largest importer of edible oils, and tax differentials (import duties) favoured importing oil over oilseed and raw oil over refined oil. The company planned a 600-ton-per-day refinery and saw supply chain management as a source of competitive advantage, with transportation making up about 70% of logistics cost. The key decisions it faced were where to locate warehouses, which transport mode to choose, and how to route shipments.
summary.question: The abstract frames the decisions the company faced: where to locate warehouses, which mode of transport to choose, and how to route shipments.

findings: India's edible oil market was estimated at 13 million tons, with imports of about 4 million tons, making India the largest importer of edible oils in the world.
A differential in duties on oilseed and oils made importing edible oils more favourable than importing oilseeds.
A differential duty between refined and raw oil encouraged importing raw oil to support domestic refineries.
Approximately 70% of the total logistics cost was accounted for by transportation cost.
summary.whyItMatters: The abstract presents supply chain management as one of the company's important means of gaining a competitive edge. Its focus on warehouse location, transport mode and routing, and on transport's large share of logistics cost, points to these choices as central for an edible oil business that depends on imports and tax differentials.
